title: Wine News: What I’m Reading the Week of 7/26/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I

The post Wine News: What I’m Reading the Week of 7/26/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I spend each week trolling the web for everything published about wine online, and here’s everything that I think would be worth your valuable time.

Highway to Hella Chenin
A review of an excellent event.

Remembering Italian Winemaker Franco Bernabei
Not well known in the US, but very influential in Tuscany.

Livermore wine families feud over Concannon ownership
A local soap opera.

Monarch Tractors Promised to Save American Wine With AI. Then, It Closed. What Happened?
Ah, the great promise of AI meets the reality of manufacturing and agricuture.

Forget Franzia—Boxed Wine Went Bougie. Now Sales Have Surged More Than 144 Percent
Slap the bag!

Sonoma County Begins One of Its Earliest Winegrape Harvests in Years
Earliest ever for many.

California’s next big wine craze is breaking all the rules
I dislike the word “blouge” but the wines are great. Is it a craze, tho?

Here’s how much regulations add to a Napa small winery’s costs, per Cal Poly
It’s a staggering sum — close to 10% of the cost of goods sold in one example.

The Champagne Fallacy
Jay McInerney can’t recommend the bath.

Fire Nears Bordeaux, a City of Wine and History
It’s serious. Friends there say, however, that it is starting to get under control.

Wildfires threaten wine city of Bordeaux as France and Spain battle blazes
More coverage. 250,000 people evacuated.

Wildfires threaten historic vineyards in Sierra de Gredos
And it’s not just Bordeaux. We don’t know the extent of the old vine losses here, yet, but it will be tragic.

Inside The French Laundry’s Wine Program: How Wine Is Selected For Every Guest
Yuri Shima goes behind the scenes.

There’s a Chablis for Every Kind of Chardonnay Lover
And even for some who think they don’t like Chardonnay.

China’s White Wine Boom Has Triggered a Marlborough Price War
And NZ Sav Blanc is on the battlefield.

title: I’ll Drink to That!: Is Cory Empting Writing The Next Chapter of Napa Valley Cabernet at Harlan Estate?
summary:
A new episode of the I’ll Drink to That! wine talk podcast was released recently. Episode 504 features Cory Empting. Cory oversees

The post I’ll Drink to That!: Is Cory Empting Writing The Next Chapter of Napa Valley Cabernet at Harlan Estate? appeared first on Vinography.
content:
A new episode of the I’ll Drink to That! wine talk podcast was released recently. Episode 504 features Cory Empting. Cory oversees Harlan Estate, BOND, Promontory, and The Mascot, all in the Napa Valley, in his role as Managing Director of Winegrowing at Domain H. William Harlan.

Wildfires threatened the lives of Cory Empting’s family in 2017. Less importantly but also significantly, they threatened the vineyards he oversees. That terrible experience altered Cory’s personal and professional priorities. Three years later, columns of smoke again arose in the Napa Valley. But it turned out that years of farming changes gave Cory an opportunity to counter the threat to the wines, and in what he calls “an inflection point” for one of America’s most famous wineries, Cory took a different approach to harvest. How do farming and resiliency intersect? This interview articulates the response to that question in a very personal way.

Episode 504 is available on many listening platforms, including at these links:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Spotify

I’ll Drink to That!, one of the world’s top wine podcasts, is hosted by Levi Dalton. Levi has had a long career working as a sommelier in some of the most distinguished and acclaimed dining rooms in America. He has served wine to guests of Restaurant Daniel, Masa, and Alto, all in Manhattan. Levi has also contributed articles on wine themes to publications such as The Art of Eating, Wine & Spirits magazine, Bon Appetit online, and Eater NY. Check out his pictures on Instagram.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/19/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/19/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week I tried two more of the current releases from Raventos i Blanc, the venerable Spanish sparkling wine producer who makes some of the most compelling sparkling wines in the Penedes region of Spain. Their dedication to single-site production and indigenous grape varieties in the region has caused them to withdraw from all of the DO organizations they might ordinarily belong to in their region, so the wines are just labeled as Spanish sparkling wines, but don’t let that fool you. These are serious bubbles. In particular, I loved the latest vintage of their De la Finca blend.

I’ve also been working my way through a bunch of Virginia wines and have several to recommend, starting with a tasty Vermentino from Barboursville Vineyards. Vermentino isn’t a grape I associate with Virginia, but this one was quite competently made. Petit Manseng, on the other hand, is one of the most successful white grapes in the region, and a taste of the bottle from The Winery at La Grange will give you an understanding of why. Nicely balanced, aromatic, and wonderfully bright, it’s a pleasure to drink.

Virginia is also known for its Bordeaux blends, and the three reds I’m recommending this week bear out that reputation. The CrossKeys Vineyards Cabernet Franc has a wonderful freshness to it and a classic profile. The Pollack Vineyards Reserve Merlot has a nice dark complexion but also some savory notes to complement the rich fruit. And the Glen Manor “Vin Rouge” offers a nice melange of herbal and blue fruit flavors along with toasted oak.

Finally, I am pleased to recommend some current and upcoming releases from Inglenook, Francis Ford Coppola’s historic estate in Napa. I reviewed their white wines last week, and this week I’m featuring their estate Cabernet Sauvignon and the top bottling they call Rubicon. The 2023 versions of both wines are fantastic, showing all the elegance that the very cool vintage had to offer. The 2024s reflect the slightly warmer year and are excellent as well, though perhaps not reaching the heights of the 2023s, at least not yet. If you enjoy the more elegant, lower-alcohol side of Napa wines, these wines will delight you.

Notes on all these follow below.

Tasting Notes

2023 Raventos i Blanc “De La Finca” White Blend, Spain
Yellow gold in the glass, with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of lemon and ripe apples with a hint of herbs. In the mouth, a voluminous mousse delivers bright floral lemon and pastry cream flavors across the palate while excellent acidity and a stony wet-pavement minerality make for an elegant, refined quality. Very pretty. A blend of 60% Xarel·lo, 30% Macabeu, and 10% Parellada fermented in stainless steel and concrete. Malolactic conversion inhibited. Secondary fermentation in the bottle, where the wine ages on the lees for 30 months. Certified organic. 12% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $39. click to buy.

2022 Raventos i Blanc “Textures de Pedra” White Blend, Spain
Bronze-gold in the glass with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of berries, herbs, and baked apples. In the mouth, a muscular mousse delivers flavors of baked apples, dried orange peel, dried herbs, and wet chalkboard as excellent acidity and a hint of salinity round out this savory experience on the palate. There’s a faint aromatic sweetness that lingers in the finish. Certified organic. A blend of Xarel·lo Vermell and Sumoll fermented and aged for 9 months in concrete. Malolactic conversion inhibited. Secondary fermentation in bottle. Aged on the lees in the bottle for 42 months. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2024 Barboursville “Reserve” Vermentino, Virginia
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of pears, white flowers, and dried herbs. In the mouth, silky flavors of pear and linalool mix with hints of herbs and a touch of citrus pith. Very good acidity and a nice chalky underbelly round out the package. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $25. click to buy.

2024 The Winery at La Grange Petit Manseng, Virginia
Light yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of honeysuckle, yellow apples, and lemon curd. In the mouth, candied lemons, apple, and a hint of pineapple are all bright and juicy thanks to excellent, even slightly electric acidity. Juicy and delicious. 13.9% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $39. click to buy.

2024 CrossKeys Vineyard Cabernet Franc, Shenandoah Valley, Virginia
Dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black plums, crushed nuts, and a hint of struck match. In the mouth, juicy and bright flavors of black plum and pencil lead are wrapped in fine, powdery tannins that coat the mouth. Excellent acidity accompanies chopped green herbs and hints of citrus peel that linger in the finish. Fresh and juicy. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $31. click to buy.

2023 Pollak Vineyards “Reserve” Merlot, Monticello, Virginia
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherries, plums, and oak. In the mouth, black cherry flavors and notes of toasted oak are wrapped in a fleecy blanket of tannins. Very good acidity offers some nice freshness as chopped green herbs and black plums linger in the finish. 14.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $60. click to buy.

2023 Glen Manor Vineyards “Vin Rouge” Red Blend, Virginia
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, prunes, and blueberries. In the mouth, black cherry and blueberry flavors are wrapped in fleecy tannins and shot through with chopped green herbs. Very good acidity gives a nice freshness to the wine, and the powdery tannins coat the mouth and linger as notes of oak emerge in the finish. A blend of 67% Cabernet Sauvignon, 19% Cabernet Franc, 10% Merlot, and 4% Petit Verdot. 13.4% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $35. click to buy.

2023 Troon Vineyard Syrah, Applegate Valley, Southern Oregon, Oregon
Medium to dark garnet in the glass with purple highlights, this wine smells of blackberries, blueberries, and a hint of horse manure. In the mouth, juicy acidity makes blackberry and blueberry flavors bright as fleecy tannins coat the mouth and darker wet earth and dried herb notes surface amongst the fruit. Dried herbs and a touch of that barnyard note linger in the finish. Excellent acidity. Demeter-certified biodynamic. Regenerative Organic Certified Gold. 12% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $44. click to buy.

2024 Inglenook Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackcurrant and black cherry with a hint of licorice and baking spices. In the mouth, blackcurrant and chopped green herbs mix with black cherry. Fine, powdery tannins coat the mouth, as chopped green herbs and dried flowers linger in the finish. Excellent acidity. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $100.

2023 Inglenook Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of chopped herbs, blueberries, blackcurrant, and violets. In the mouth, smooth powdery tannins coat the mouth and surround a core of black cherry, blackcurrant, a hint of licorice root, and chopped green herbs. Excellent acidity, floral perfume, and a lovely roundness to the wine. 14.3% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $100. click to buy.

2024 Inglenook “Rubicon” Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackcurrant and black cherries. In the mouth, mouthwatering acidity makes for a juicy character in plum, blackcurrant, and black cherry fruit. Powdery, even stony tannins coat the mouth but remain supple through the finish. Dried herbs and freshly chopped herbs linger in the finish. 14.2% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $265.

2023 Inglenook “Rubicon” Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of blackcurrant, plums, and black cherries with a hint of mocha. In the mouth, black cherry and blackcurrant flavors mix with dried flowers and plums. Seamless, supple tannins coat the mouth, and give a wonderful shape to the wine. Notes of licorice and violets linger in the finish. Excellent, juicy acidity. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $265. click to buy.

title: Vinography Images: Spare Vines
summary:
The Savennières appellation is one of the Loire’s smallest, both in its overall size (roughly 350 hectares) and in its

The post Vinography Images: Spare Vines appeared first on Vinography.
content:
The Savennières appellation is one of the Loire’s smallest, both in its overall size (roughly 350 hectares) and in its plantings, as only around 170 of those hectares are planted. Consequently, there’s no such thing as a spare vine when it comes to the region’s energetic and delicious Chenin Blanc. These two vines out front at Domaine du Closel might look ornamental, but they get harvested every year.

title: Unfiltered Wine Festival: July 25-26, Berkeley
summary:
You know what’s better than a wine tasting event that features some really excellent producers of low-intervention wines? Two days

The post Unfiltered Wine Festival: July 25-26, Berkeley appeared first on Vinography.
content:
You know what’s better than a wine tasting event that features some really excellent producers of low-intervention wines? Two days of that kind of event plus some thought-provoking panel sessions to go along with it.

That’s what you’re going to get this coming weekend with the Unfiltered Wine Festival hosted at Donkey & Goat Winery in Berkeley. Billed as “A Celebration of Wine on the Edge,” this event features a number of my favorite California wineries pouring their stuff, and some very interesting topics for discussion.

The panel sessions include: “Breaking the Champagne Spell: California’s Great Sparkling Wine Experiment,” “From Chad Hinds’ ‘Psychic Terroir’ to Vinyl Listening Bars: Recentering The Experiencial Value of Wine Through Music,” “An Essential and Elusive Grail: Imagining the Future of California Table Wine,” “Natural vs. Conventional: Where Is The Line and Why Does It Matter?” “The Lodi Effect: How Did Lodi Become a Hotbed for Creativity in Wine?” and “What Makes A Great Wine: Restraint versus Risk.”

The panelists for these talks are some of the who’s-who of California wine producers, plus journalists, sommeliers, and more.

Here is the list of producers scheduled to pour during the two days of the festival:

Saturday, July 25th

AmByth Estate, Analog Wine Co., Caleb Leisure, Clos Saron, Donkey & Goat, Driftwood Cottage, En Cavale, Feral Ecology, Forlorn Hope, Frenchtown Farms, Fres.co Wine, Ghostnote, Grenachista, Ian Brand Wines, Inter Tidal Wines, Iruai Wine, Joseph‑Jibril, Lula, Matt Crutchfield Wines, Onward Wines, Prima Materia, Reclamation Wines, Rootdown Cellars, Spur Road, Thee And Thou Wines, A Tribute to Grace, Unturned Stone, Vine Farm Ridge, Volta, Wonderwerk.

Sunday, July 26th

280 Project, Arcadian, Bedrock, Ellsworth Wines, Enfield, Etteilla Wines, Gondak Cellars, Haarmeyer Wine, Helia Wine Co., Hovik Wine, Mad Marvlus Wine, Madson Wines, Maison Des Plaisances, Minus Tide Wines, Native Bloom Winery, Newfound Wines, Ottavino Wines, Popelouchum Estate, Precedent, Ruby Blanca, Ruth Lewandowski, Ryme Cellars, Samuel Louis Smith, Schema Wines, Ser Wines, Stagiaire Wine, Trail Marker Wine, Virgo Magic, Ward Four.

These are all independent, vision-driven, high-integrity winemakers. Some are newcomers, others have been leading the way for decades. Some are unabashed natural winemakers, while many believe in the judicious use of sulfur dioxide. Regardless, there’s lots of tasty juice on offer during each day.

In short, not a bad way to spend a couple of weekend afternoons!

2026 Unfiltered Wine Festival
Saturday, July 25 and Sunday, July 26
1:00 PM – 5:00 PM both days
Donkey & Goat Winery
1340 Fifth St
Berkeley, CA 94710 (map)

Tickets for each day will run you $65, with a two-day pass price of $95. Purchase tickets online.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/12/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/12/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week included a couple of Napa’s best white wines in the form of the two made by Inglenook, the historic estate that has been painstakingly resurrected by the team working for owner Francis Ford Coppola. Their Sauvignon Blanc is positively stellar, certainly one of the best in the valley, and their more oak-inflected, Bordeaux-style white blend is also excellent. I highly recommend both, and (in the bizarro world of Napa pricing) they’re both quite affordable.

The folks from Tasca d’Almerita in Sicily sent through a couple of bottles last week, their Etna Bianco and Etna Rosso wines from the Tenuta Tascante brand. Both are fresh, stony, and aromatic as many such wines from the volcano are. They’re also nice values as they can both be found for under $30 apiece.

I’ve also got two more white wines from Gainey Vineyard in the Santa Ynez Valley to recommend this week: their Sauvignon Gris, which has a very nice tropical quality, as well as their Chardonnay, which had just a touch more wood than I would like. Their estate Syrah also has its modicum of wood, but offers nice black fruits and good acidity that many will find appealing.

I also got a couple of new releases from the irrepressible Randall Grahm and his magnum opus of a vineyard he planted from seed, called Popelouchum. One of them, which he simply calls “Popelouchum Blanc,” might well be the best white wine I’ve ever had from his hands. It’s a lovely blend of Grenache Blanc and Grenache Gris, and wonderfully delicious with a slightly flinty reductive character that is very appealing. The other wine, his “Exuberance” Pinot Noir, will appeal to those who enjoy more savory, herbal-inflected Pinot Noirs.

Finally, I’ve got a few wines from Virginia to recommend this week. The first is a Meritage (a proprietary term for wines made in the Bordeaux tradition that must contain at least two grape varieties and no more than 90% of them). The one I tasted this past week was mostly Merlot and Petit Verdot from 7 Lady Vineyards, and the tannins certainly wouldn’t let you forget about the Petit Verdot. But there was some nice freshness there, too, though the nasty, heavy bottle was a big turn-off, environmentally speaking.

The Michael Shaps Cabernet Franc offered a nice balance of berry and herbal tones with a strong note of oak and a touch of reduction, while the Valley Road Vineyards reserve Cabernet Franc was wonderfully fresh and balanced, making it perhaps one of the best Virginia wines I’ve had in a long while.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

2024 Inglenook Sauvignon Blanc, Rutherford, Napa, California
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, lemon juice, green apple, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, sour green apple, kiwi fruit, and lime juice flavors have a fantastic mouthwatering acidity and faint salinity. There’s a light chalky texture. Wonderfully fresh and delicious. 13% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $40. click to buy.

2024 Inglenook “Blancaneaux” White Blend, Rutherford, Napa, California
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of vanilla, pears, and white peaches. In the mouth, wonderfully bright pear and white peach flavors have a stony breadth and crispness. There’s a faint saline quality here, along with a chalky texture lingering in the finish. Lovely freshness. 13.8% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $57. click to buy.

2025 Tascante “Buonora” White Blend, Etna, Sicily, Italy
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lime zest, white flowers, and sea air. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon pith and lime pith mix with pomelo and a hint of jasmine, as bright acidity keeps things juicy and vibrant on the palate. There’s a light wet pavement quality in the finish. Certified B Corp. Certified Sustainable. 12% alcohol. Closed with a technical (resin) cork. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2025 Gainey Vineyard “Limited Selection” Sauvignon Gris, Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Barbara, California
Palest straw in the glass, this wine smells of passionfruit, star fruit, and green apples. In the mouth, green guava and passionfruit flavors are bright with excellent, even sharp acidity that puckers the cheeks and makes the mouth water. There’s a faint nutty quality that emerges in the finish. Whole-cluster pressed and fermented in neutral oak. Aged briefly in stainless steel before bottling. 388 cases made. 12.9% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $40.

2024 Gainey Vineyard “Limited Selection” Chardonnay, Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Barbara, California
Light gold in the glass with a hint of green, this wine smells of lemon curd, toasted nuts, and pastry cream. In the mouth, toasted oak flavors mix with lemon peel and lemon pith, and excellent acidity keeps the mouth watering. Roasted nuts and a faint salinity linger in the finish. Slightly more wood than I would like here, but this wine has good energy and dynamism. Whole-cluster pressed, settled overnight, and then barrel fermented. Aged for 10 months in 33% new French oak. 881 cases made. 14.1% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $48. click to buy.

2023 Popelouchum “Blanc” White Blend, San Benito, Central Coast, California
Light bronze-gold in color, this wine smells of slightly resinous lemon peel, apple, and pink grapefruit. In the mouth, wonderfully zingy and bright flavors of grapefruit, white nectarine, and lemon pith are faintly saline and very mouthwatering thanks to excellent acidity. There’s a hint of reductive gunflint here that is quite charming. A blend of 60% Grenache Blanc and 40% Grenache Gris that is extremely delicious. This might be the best white wine I’ve ever had from Randall Grahm. 300 cases made. Closed with a screwcap. Score: around 9. Cost: $45.

2023 Popelouchum “Exuberance” Pinot Noir, San Benito, Central Coast, California
Light ruby in the glass with garnet highlights, this wine smells of wet redwood bark, potting soil, and cranberries. In the mouth, cranberry and wet earth flavors mix with sawdust and dried herbs. Decent acidity and faint gauzy tannins accompany notes of chopped green herbs that linger in the finish. Very savory. 12.5% alcohol. 170 cases made. Closed with a screwcap. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $65.

2024 Tascante “Ghaia Nera” Red Blend, Etna, Sicily, Italy
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of red berries, wet pavement, and dried herbs. In the mouth, powdered stone tannins coat the mouth as flavors of sour cherry, strawberry, and cranberry mix with dried herbs and a hint of struck match. The tannins stiffen with time and remain very stony. Certified B Corp. Certified Sustainable. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2024 Gainey Vineyard Syrah, Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Barbara, California
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, wet pavement, and dried herbs. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of blackberry, wet earth, and a hint of sweet oak. Excellent acidity keeps things fresh on the palate, while the sweet oak dominates the finish. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $??

2023 7 Lady Vineyards Meritage, Virginia
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherry, molasses, licorice, and blackberries. In the mouth, deep and earthy flavors of black cherry and licorice are wrapped in a thick fleecy blanket of tannins and shot through with very good acidity. A minty quality of chopped herbs lingers in the finish. Brawny, but with a nice freshness. A blend of 44% Merlot, 37% Petit Verdot, and 19% Cabernet Franc. 13.9% alcohol. Comes in an egregiously heavy bottle weighing 1.75 kg when full, which means the bottle itself weighs a kilogram. Rather shameful from an environmental perspective. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $65.

2023 Michael Shaps Cabernet Franc, Virginia
Dark garnet in color, this wine smells of struck match, plum, and plum skin. In the mouth, plum and dried herb flavors are wrapped in a fleecy blanket of tannin. Notes of oak and espresso emerge in the finish along with a hint of struck match. Decent acidity, but perhaps just a little too much wood here. 13.7% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $34. click to buy.

2023 Valley Road Vineyards “Reserve” Cabernet Franc, Monticello, Virginia
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of plum, berries, and cherries. In the mouth, fresh and juicy flavors of plum and cherry are shot through with dried and freshly chopped herbs as fine tannins coat the mouth and stiffen slightly in the finish. Clean, bright, with a lovely balance. 13.7% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $42.

Joly makes wines of another age, as the ancient farm implements suggest, and the cow horns make the biodynamic focus clear. You’re likely to be greeted by a member of the family, and then sit down to taste wines unlike any others in the region.

Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I spend each week trolling the web for everything published about wine online, and here’s everything that I think would be worth your valuable time.

Climate change could redraw California wine country maps
It already has. The maps haven’t caught up.

Why Peru Is Becoming South America’s Most Exciting Wine and Spirit Destination
Kathleen Willcox is everywhere.

Michelin is about to do for wine what it did for food – ruin it
Tell us how you really feel Victoria Moore (you go, girl!).

Will Canada end up being punished for the US alcohol ban?
The US is pissed that when we threw a tantrum, Canada took its toys and left. SMH.

When Napa met Bordeaux
Jancis on Opus One.

To make wine is to believe in the future: the Ukrainians growing grapes on the frontline
Bravery. Faith. We need to keep telling these stories.

Hollywood actor turned winemaker Sam Neill passes away
A tragic loss for wine. And also for film. But many of us in the wine world knew him not as a celebrity but as a farmer.

The Marginal Acre
Ted goes out into the vineyard with this one.

How Weight Loss is Hitting Wine
Liza B. Zimmerman looks into the little data that is out there.

Yoichi, Hokkaidō: A Growing Destination for Wine Lovers
On the bucket list for sure.

Mourvèdre Was Made for Heat. Rising Temperatures Are Testing It
Everything is fine, we said, from amongst the flames.

Jamie Goode: Tasting notes – do they matter?
Jamie wants to use a sawed-off shotgun.

Extreme Heat Can Make Alcohol Hit Harder Than You Expect
Helpful reading while we all simmer away this summer.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/5/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 7/5/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

Let’s start off this week with a wonderfully tropical Sauvignon Blanc from Refugio Ranch in Santa Barbara’s Santa Ynez Valley. It’s got a fun hint of the green guava candies you get at some Chinese restaurants, and will make most Sav Blanc lovers very happy on a summer’s day, especially when chilled down properly.

Before Chardonnay was the next big thing from Oregon, most people thought Pinot Gris was Oregon’s great hope in the white wine department. There are still some excellent ones there, hanging out in the shadows now that the spotlight has turned to Chardonnay. Domaine Divio make a tasty one that they cheekily call Pinot Beurot, the Burgundian name for the grape.

A bit farther south in Oregon, the folks at Troon Vineyard have been busy perfecting Vermentino, which is much better than some varieties at handling the heat and drought that climate change is throwing at growers everywhere. Their rendition of the grape has great acidity and a lovely fruit profile.

I’ve got two more wines from Mascarin Vineyards to recommend this week, their Estate Chardonnay from the Sonoma Coast – which has a nice waxy crispness to it – and their rosé of Pinot Noir, which has all the right flavors you want from Pinot Rosé, if perhaps slightly less acidity than ideal.

I was a bit more excited by the rosé from the folks at Minus Tide, whose Carignan Rosé from old vines in Mendocino consistently delivers racy crispness along with compelling berry and citrus peel flavors. If you like your rosé stony, savory, and electric, this one is for you.

Last week I began reviewing the latest single-vineyard Pinot Noir from Ross Cobb, and this week I’ll finish them up. I have four wines to recommend to you (highly). All demonstrate Cobb’s textbook finesse and elegance, but perhaps none so much as his Coastlands bottling, which is luminous in its herbal, berry, and citrus brightness. If you are in the market for top-end Coastal Pinot Noir, Cobb’s 2023s are worth seeking out for sure.

I personally think there is not nearly enough Gamay planted and made in California, given our predilection for and success with Pinot Noir. Apparently the folks at Presqu’ile down in Santa Barbara agree, as they’ve planted some and are making one that has a distinctly herbal character, no doubt with a decent amount of whole cluster used in its processing. If you’re into crunchy chilled reds, this one might be for you.

Finally, the folks at Spottswoode have released their latest bottling of Lyndenhurst, which I generally consider to be their slightly more approachable, early-drinking bottling of Cabernet Sauvignon. Well, in 2023, they’ve managed to make a wine that is a bit more serious than normal, and for the first time I’m recommending that instead of just opening it up and enjoying whenever, that you give it a couple of years to truly show its best.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Refugio Ranch “Tiradora” Sauvignon Blanc, Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Barbara, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, passionfruit, and guava. In the mouth, silky flavors of guava and passionfruit are bright and tropical, with decent acidity and a nice chalky texture underneath. 14.1% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2025 Domaine Divio Pinot Beurot, Willamette Valley, Oregon
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of pears, white flowers, and lemon pith. In the mouth, pears and white flowers mix with a hint of pastry cream as a faint chalky texture and very good acidity round out a tasty package. Pinot Beurot is the Burgundian name for Pinot Gris. 12.9% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $40. click to buy.

2025 Troon Vineyard Vermentino, Applegate Valley, Southern Oregon
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of rising bread dough, pears, and white flowers. In the mouth, pear and pear skin flavors mix with a hint of lemon pith and white flowers. Faintly saline in quality, with a nice stony wet-chalkboard minerality and excellent acidity. Demeter-certified biodynamic. Regenerative Organic Certified Gold. Fermented with ambient yeasts. 11.9% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $31. click to buy.

2023 Mascarin “Dalya Estate Vineyard” Chardonnay, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale to light yellow gold in color, this wine smells of lemon curd, cooked apple, resinous herbs, and a hint of struck match. In the mouth, saline, even briny flavors of lemon peel, lemon curd, and grapefruit are bright with excellent acidity and touched with a hint of toasted nuts and baked apple. There’s a zesty, even waxy intensity to this wine that is interesting. 13.1% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $60. click to buy.

2025 Minus Tide “Trimble Ranch” Rosé of Carignan, Mendocino County, California
Pale baby pink in color, this wine smells of rosehips, rhubarb, and raspberries. In the mouth, rhubarb, chopped green herbs, and redcurrant flavors are bright and juicy with tangy acidity. There’s a light chalky quality that lingers in the finish. 13.3% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $27. click to buy.

2024 Mascarin “7 Mules Vineyard” Rosé of Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Palest peachy pink in color, this wine smells of watermelon and raspberries. In the mouth, citrus peel, watermelon rind, and faint cranberry notes are zippy with acidity and faintly chalky in texture. Decent acidity. 13.6% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30.

2023 Cobb “Rice Spivak” Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet earth, redwood bark, cherries, and a touch of blood orange. In the mouth, fleecy tannins coat the mouth and become slightly muscular as flavors of cherries, forest floor, sour cherries, and raspberries are bright with excellent acidity. On the richer side for Cobb, but still impeccably balanced. Citrus peel and dried herbs linger in the finish with a hint of oak. 14% alcohol. 40% whole cluster. 230 cases made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $80. click to buy.

2023 Cobb “Doc’s Ranch – Swan and Calera Selections” Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium ruby in the glass with garnet highlights, this wine smells of wet pavement, conifer boughs, dried herbs, and raspberries. In the mouth, powdery, gauzy tannins wrap around a core of dried herbs, citrus peel, raspberries, and road dust. There’s a chalky quality to this wine, with hints of citrus peel and oak lingering in the finish. 13% alcohol. 50% whole cluster. 150 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $100. click to buy.

2023 Cobb “Coastlands Vineyard” Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium ruby in the glass with garnet highlights, this wine smells of conifer boughs, flowers, and sour cherries. In the mouth, saline sour cherries and raspberry flavors mix with citrus peel, dried flowers, and fine, powdery tannins. There’s a lovely freshness to the wine as well, thanks in part to excellent acidity but also thanks to a hint of chopped green herbs underneath everything. Balanced and dynamic with a lovely mix of savory and fruit. 13.2% alcohol. 500 cases made. 50% whole cluster. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $90. click to buy.

2023 Cobb “Coastlands Vineyard – Old Firs Block” Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of dried herbs and flowers, sour cherries, and redcurrants. In the mouth, powdery tannins coat the mouth and stiffen slightly to surround a core of raspberries and redcurrants shot through with sweet oak and citrus peel. There’s a chalky quality to this wine and the tannins dry the mouth slightly. Excellent acidity. 12.7% alcohol. 50% whole cluster. 225 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $100. click to buy.

2025 Presqu’ile Gamay, Santa Maria Valley, Santa Barbara, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of marijuana, chopped green cooking herbs, and blood oranges. In the mouth, blood orange and cherry flavors are shot through with bitter greens and chopped herbs. Fleecy tannins coat the top of the mouth as excellent acidity keeps things juicy. Very savory in character with herbs almost more dominant than the fruit. SIP Certified sustainable, practicing organic. Fermented in stainless steel with ambient yeasts. Aged 6 months in neutral French oak. 13% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $38.

2023 Spottswoode “Lyndenhurst” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, blackcurrant, and sweet oak. In the mouth, juicy blackcurrant and blackcurrant leaf flavors mix with black cherries and sweet oak as fleecy, supple tannins coat the mouth. Fantastic acidity offers lots of freshness, and though this is the early-drinking bottling from this vineyard, I would suggest 3 to 5 years of bottle age for optimum enjoyment. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $110. click to buy.
